newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST-Australia to extend record GDP run.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST-Australia to extend record GDP run.

text.p: Australia is expected to extend its record run of 21 quarters of uninterrupted growth in the December quarter, with earlier concerns of flat or even negative growth eased by a run of strong partial indicators, economists said.

Wednesday's gross domestic product (GDP) data is expected to show the economy continued its moderate pace of growth in the final quarter of 1996, with many seeing the second half or the year as the soft point in growth for the current cycle.
Median forecasts of the 26 economists surveyed by Reuters after Monday's inventories data are for a 0.6 percent quarterly rise, with annual growth forecast at 3.6 percent.

"The data are rather dated but it is worth noting that it is becoming increasingly clear that the low point in the Australian growth slowdown occurred during mid to late 1996 when it appears that the growth pulse fell to around 2.5-3.0 percent," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economists said in a commentary.
An interesting feature of GDP forecasts is that they have edged higher through the month leading up to their release.
"It was not that long ago that market forecasts for the December quarter GDP(A) were for a flat result, but now most biases are to the upside," Citibank Australia economists said.
After December quarter retail trade fell 1.3 percent, economists forecasts centred on a 0.3 percent quarterly rise, with some forecasting flat or negative growth.
However, after the release of investment and company profits data the median forecast had lifted to 0.5 percent last Friday.
Monday's release of business inventories data, showing sizeable revisions to previous quarters, saw the size of the expected detraction from GDP scaled back and forecasts firm.
Economists said the risk on the 0.6 percent quarterly forecast is to the upside, with government spending expected to contribute to growth after a weak September quarter.

Income based GDP is expected to be the strongest of the three measures, with strong growth in company profits and wages, salaries and supplements expected. GDP(I) was also the strongest measure in the September quarter.
Expenditure based GDP is generally seen being the weakest measure, weighed on by the weak private consumption, an expected detraction by net exports and housing.
The revisions to inventories suggest only a small detraction, while investment and public spending should be positive.
Production based GDP is always the hardest component to forecast, but is seen as positive, with potential seen for upward revisions to the agricultural sector forecasts.
The breakdown of growth reflects the patchy performance of the economy in 1996, economists said.

"The aggregate outcome was cushioned by the desynchronised nature of growth across sectors, such as housing, experiencing lower output but other sectors, such as business investment, experiencing strong gains," the DMG economists said.
One of the biggest surprises in the September quarter GDP was the negative 0.4 percent GDP(E) deflator, which underlined the favourable inflation performance.

The median forecast is for a 0.4 percent rise in the December quarter which economists said did not not represent a quickening in inflation so much as just a reflection that the September quarter data probably understated the level of inflation.
Looking further ahead, economists share the optimism of the Reserve Bank that growth will firm through 1997 and said it could be approaching four percent in annual terms by year end.
"Quarterly outcomes for 1997 should be higher and the mix of growth should be more favourable," GIO Australia chief economist Akis Haralabopoulos said. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
